program_identity.mission: To provide students with the needed knowledge and skills in electrical engineering, to conduct scientific research, and to contribute to the sustainability of the society.

educational_objectives.PEO1: Technical Competence and Innovation- EE graduates will apply electrical engineering knowledge and skills to design solutions, solve complex problems, and pursue graduate studies and research, demonstrating creativity and innovation.
educational_objectives.PEO2: Ethical, Professional, and Sustainable Responsibilities- EE graduates will uphold ethical standards, commit to sustainability, and pursue lifelong learning.
educational_objectives.PEO3: Leadership and Teamwork- EE graduates will demonstrate leadership, critical thinking, decision-making, and teamwork, contributing positively to their organizations and society.

clos.clo_text: Explain fundamental electrical quantities, circuit elements, and basic AC signal concepts and their relationships in linear circuits.

courses.course_description: This module provides a comprehensive introduction to both DC and AC circuit principles. Students will begin by reviewing fundamental concepts, including current, voltage, and power. The course then explores series and parallel circuits and delves into Ohm’s Law, Kirchhoff’s Laws, source transformations, bridge networks, and delta/star transformations. Key analysis methods and network theorems are also covered. Additionally, the module revisits inductors and capacitors, introduces sinusoidal sources and the concept of phasors, and details methods for analyzing AC circuits. Practical experience is emphasized through hands-on use of electrical measurement tools such as voltmeters, ammeters, wattmeters, function generators, and oscilloscopes.
courses.prerequisite_text: PHYS 205, Math113
course_objectives: Understand the basic linear electric circuits, theories, and concepts.
Understand circuit theorems and laws of circuit analysis in DC and AC circuits.
Gain hands-on experience and develop skills in using measurement tools like voltmeters, ammeters, and oscilloscopes while linking theory to practice.

courses.course_description: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to essential semiconductor devices and amplifiers. It covers diodes, including special-purpose types, and explores Bipolar Junction Transistors (BJTs) with a focus on their operation, characteristics, and various biasing methods. Students will study transistor amplifier configurations such as common emitter, common collector, and common base, as well as classes of power amplifiers. The course also delves into operational amplifiers (Op-Amps), addressing their parameters, feedback mechanisms, and various practical circuit applications.

courses.course_description: The course begins by reviewing the behaviors of inductor and capacitor storing elements. It then covers the characteristics and behavior of first-order RL/RC circuits, as well as second-order RLC circuits. Additionally, the course explains the conversion of time-domain circuits to the s-domain using the Laplace transform. Furthermore, it delves into frequency response and resonance, providing a basic understanding of filter circuits. The course also includes the study of electrical configurations involving three phases of networks and the analysis of two-port networks.

courses.course_description: In this course, we focus on signal transforms and continuous-wave modulation, which is the basic operation of analog communication systems. Initially, we give the students an insight and understanding of signals classifications, Fourier series, Fourier transform, spectrum analysis, and explore their applications in the context of analog communication systems. We then cover thoroughly amplitude modulation including the generation and reception of double-side band, single side-band, and vestigial side-band. We also cover the angle modulations (phase and frequency), the generation both the narrow and wide-band angle modulation.
course_objectives: Introduce topics of signal spectrum analysis, modulation/demodulation, pulse modulation techniques, and design tradeoffs.
Evaluate the characteristics of different classes of signals, and produce their representation in both time and frequency domains.
Provide knowledge of analog modulation techniques and their comparative analysis and applications suitability.
textbooks: Lathi, Modern Digital and Analog Communication Systems, Fifth Edition, Oxford University Press, 2018.

The course is focused on the applications of the power converter in various sectors, e.g., industrial, electric grid, renewable energy, microgrid, electric vehicle, etc. In addition, the course covers the basic characteristics, control schemes, and applications of power semiconductor devices and circuits.

courses.course_description: Cooperative Education is a planned learning experience, for which credits are earned, that integrates classroom theory and learning experiences at a workplace. The experience enables students to apply and refine the knowledge and skills acquired in a related curriculum course. The Co-op is a supervised work experience in a position in the government or the private sector which aimed to assist students in making the transition from the classroom to industry. Students are required to finish 28 weeks on the job to earn 10-credit hours for the course

courses.course_description: This course offers an introduction to Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) design, exposing students to the complexities of creating integrated circuits with cutting-edge technologies. It begins with an exploration of VLSI systems, outlining key design and fabrication stages, including ASIC and FPGA development and processes like photolithography. Participants will explore significant industry players and evolving market trends and gain practical skills through extensive use of HDLs like VHDL and Verilog for circuit design and simulation. The curriculum also covers functional and timing analysis, post-synthesis optimization, and various packaging technologies. Additionally, the course addresses professional ethics in VLSI design, stressing regulatory adherence, intellectual property integrity, accurate reporting, and environmental awareness, equipping students for the technical and ethical challenges in the semiconductor industry.
courses.prerequisite_text: Senior level standing (completion of 90 credit hours)

clos.clo_text: Explain the operating principles and performance characteristics of electronic circuits and subsystems used in communication transmitters and receivers.
Analyze the performance of communication electronic circuits using appropriate circuit, semiconductor, and signal principles.
Design communication electronic circuits or subsystems for specified performance requirements.
Communicate the analysis, design, and performance of communication electronic circuits through technical reports and presentations.
Characterize the performance of communication electronic circuits through simulation and laboratory measurement.
Apply newly acquired knowledge to emerging devices, circuits, and technologies in communication electronics.

courses.prerequisite_text: Senior level standing (completion of 90 credit hours)

clos.clo_text: Understand basic data communication and network concepts and protocols
Implement and evaluate middle-layer data access protocols
Integrate Smart Systems with cloud-based networking solutions

courses.course_description: This course provides a comprehensive understanding of data communication networks with a strong focus on data communication and networking techniques for smart system applications such smart grids, energy systems for smart homes, buildings and factories. It covers network architectures, protocols, and data transmission principles, emphasizing wireless and wired communication technologies essential for Smart systems applications. The course covers several protocols operating at different layers of OSI and TCP/IP models. The course will focus on implementing Middle layer data access layer protocols (MQTT/CoAP etc), to provide real-time data communication, and networking for IoT-enabled smart systems. The course also explores Smart System integration with cloud-based application layers. It also covers data communication fundamentals, such as modulation, error correction, and synchronization techniques relevant to real-time Smart Systems applications.
courses.prerequisite_text: Senior level standing (completion of 90 credit hours)

clos.clo_text: Recognize the source and channel coding theorems.
Explain the notions of entropy, relative entropy and mutual information, and how they are relevant.
Calculate the capacity of different channels.
Analyze and design source and channel coding schemes.

courses.course_description: This course addresses the problem of designing efficient and reliable digital communication systems through introducing the field of information theory. Source and channel coding which are important elements of information theory are essential for any communication systems. We cover the mathematical preliminaries related to those elements, such as entropy, relative entropy, and mutual information. We show how they arise as natural answers to questions of data compression, channel capacity, and error correction. We also study different source and channel coding schemes, such as Huffman, arithmetic, block, cyclic, and convolution codes.
courses.prerequisite_text: Senior level standing (completion of 90 credit hours)

clos.clo_text: Explain fundamental wireless communication principles
Describe the challenges in designing the physical and link layers of wireless systems.
Apply digital modulation and multiple access techniques
Design wireless system components

courses.course_description: This course explores the technical challenges and solutions in designing the physical and link layers of wireless communication systems. Key topics include wireless channel characterization, cellular network principles, digital modulation methods, spread spectrum, and multiple access techniques such as CDMA and OFDMA. The course also covers diversity techniques and introduces advanced technologies like LTE, MIMO, and 5G NR.
courses.prerequisite_text: Senior level standing (completion of 90 credit hours)

clos.clo_text: Describe electomagnetic wave radiation mechanism.
Recognize various antennas types
Design antennas for various applications.
Design and analyze antenna arrays.
Calculate antenna parameters like gain, input impedance, radiated power and radiation resistance.
Describe electromagnetic interference, radiation hazards, and the effect of EM fields on the environment.

courses.course_description: This course provides the students with an understanding of the basic principles of Antenna Analysis and Design, an overview of the fundamental characteristics and parameters of antennas, an overview of analytical and numerical methods used to analyze and design antennas with application to some basic antenna structures such as linear antennas, loop antennas, and antenna arrays.
courses.prerequisite_text: Senior level standing (completion of 90 credit hours)

clos.clo_text: Understand the concept of mechatronic system design and how to construct a conceptual framework to select an appropriate solution approach
Learn how to work with sensors, actuators, controllers and how to read and interpret data sheets.
Learn how to model and simulate mechatronic systems and how to verify design solutions before their implementation.
Write technical reports following a well-defined design procedure

courses.course_description: This course provides a multidisciplinary introduction to Mechatronics, focusing on the synergetic integration of mechanical systems, electronics, sensors, actuators, microcontrollers, and information technology to create intelligent automation solutions. It starts with thinking how the required function can be realized by the combination of different subsystems according to a Systems Engineering approach (V-model). Students will explore electro-mechanical systems controlled by microcontrollers, gaining hands-on experience in instrumentation, measurement systems, data acquisition, and control techniques. Through practical applications, students will learn how to design, implement, and troubleshoot sensor-actuator systems, interface microcontrollers with real-world mechanisms, and develop automated control solutions.
courses.prerequisite_text: Senior level standing (completion of 90 credit hours)

clos.clo_text: Describe fundamental automation and control concepts related to programmable logic controllers and relay ladder logic.
Explain PLC hardware structure, programming concepts, and industrial applications using appropriate technical terminology, ladder diagrams, and documentation.
Conduct laboratory experiments involving PLC programming, testing, and monitoring to evaluate system behavior and performance.
Apply new PLC functions, instructions, and communication concepts using manuals, software tools, and self-directed learning resources.

courses.course_description: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs), equipping students with both theoretical knowledge and hands-on experience in industrial automation. Students will explore the core principles of PLC operation, including relay ladder logic programming, and gain practical exposure to real-world industrial applications. Through interactive lab exercises and case studies, students will learn about the structure and functionality of PLCs, covering I/O modules, relays, counters, timers, and data manipulation techniques. Additionally, students will examine how PLCs integrate into modern automated manufacturing systems and explore their role in industrial networking and smart factory solutions.
courses.prerequisite_text: Senior level standing (completion of 90 credit hours)

clos.clo_text: Describe the basic theory underlying modern robotics
Analyze the kinematics and dynamics of robot manipulators
Design appropriate controllers and trajectory generation solutions for manipulators
Comply to safety considerations in the design and operation of robotic systems
Contribute responsibly to team-based planning and problem-solving in a group robotics project.

courses.course_description: This course has basic Python programming as a prerequisite. The course delivers fundamental concepts of robotics and automation, designed for electrical engineering students those has basic Python knowledge. The course covers, topics those are essentials to build robots, including actuators, sensors, robot kinematics, control systems, and automation technologies. Furthermore, the course will provide insights into robot motion, position and force control, and mobile robotics. The course will also explores robotic operating systems (ROS), industrial robotics, vision systems, and automation techniques used in manufacturing and smart systems. The course is designed to be applied in nature, enabling students to use python to programming automation and robotics sensors, motion planning, and AI-driven control mechanisms, preparing them for real-world applications in robotics and industrial automation.
courses.prerequisite_text: Senior level standing (completion of 90 credit hours)

clos.clo_text: Describe the theoretical foundations of supervised, unsupervised, and deep learning techniques
Analyse and prepare data for AI applications in engineering contexts.
Design AI models using appropriate metrics and interpret their results.
Write Programming Code to Implement AI models.
Use AI concepts in engineering applications such as energy prediction, automation, and intelligent control systems

courses.course_description: This course provides an introduction of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for Electrical Engineering students. This AI course covers basic AI concepts, including problem-solving techniques, search algorithms, machine learning, and knowledge representation, where the main focus will be on practical applications in electrical engineering. The course integrates hands-on experience with Python-based AI tools such as NumPy, Pandas, Scikit-Learn, and TensorFlow. Specific applications include load forecasting in power systems, AI-based signal processing, and control system optimization. By the end of the course, students will learn about theoretical knowledge and practical skills to apply AI techniques to real-world electrical engineering problems, preparing them for advanced AI applications and research in intelligent automation, smart grids, and predictive maintenance.
courses.prerequisite_text: Senior level standing (completion of 90 credit hours)

clos.clo_text: Demonstrate the role of DSP in communications, audio processing, and radar systems.
Analyze and manipulate discrete-time signals using time-domain and frequency-domain techniques.
Implement Z-transform, DFT, and FFT for efficient signal analysis.
Desgn and implement digital FIR and IIR filters for various signal processing applications.
Apply sampling and reconstruction techniques in real-world scenarios.
Utilize MATLAB for signal processing simulation and visualization.

courses.course_description: This course provides an in-depth understanding of Digital Signal Processing (DSP), focusing on the analysis, manipulation, and implementation of digital signals in various engineering applications. Students will explore discrete-time signals and systems, sampling theory, discrete Fourier transform (DFT), fast Fourier transform (FFT), digital filter design, and real-time signal processing techniques. The course emphasizes both theoretical concepts and practical implementation, preparing students for advanced topics in signal processing.
courses.prerequisite_text: Senior level standing (completion of 90 credit hours)

clos.clo_text: Explain the principles, objectives, criteria, and constraints of electric power system planning.
Analyze electrical demand and planning data using appropriate forecasting, engineering, and economic techniques.
Develop power system planning alternatives for specified technical, economic, and reliability requirements.
Communicate power system planning assumptions, analyses, results, and recommendations through technical reports and presentations.
Apply newly acquired knowledge to emerging challenges and technologies in power system planning.

courses.prerequisite_text: Senior level standing (completion of 90 credit hours)

clos.clo_text: Explain the basic concepts, components, and principles of Renewable Energy sources
Design and develop the photovoltaic and wind energy systems.
Explain the Fuel Cell systems and energy storage devices.
Illustrate the importance of energy transition and sustainability

courses.course_description: This course focuses on the principles, technologies, and applications of solar and wind energy systems. It covers energy conversion, system design, efficiency analysis, and integration into power grids. Students will explore key challenges, sustainability considerations, and advancements in photovoltaic (PV) systems and wind turbine technology. The course combines theoretical knowledge with hands-on applications to prepare students for careers in the renewable energy sector.
courses.prerequisite_text: Senior level standing (completion of 90 credit hours)

courses.course_title: Special Topics In Electrical and Electronics Engineering

clos.clo_text: Explain advanced concepts and principles related to a selected contemporary topic in electrical and electronics engineering.
Analyze engineering problems associated with the selected topic using appropriate theoretical and computational methods.
Apply relevant engineering tools, techniques, or methodologies to investigate problems related to the selected topic.
Evaluate alternative approaches, technologies, or solutions within the selected topic using appropriate technical criteria.
Develop a solution, model, system, or study addressing a problem related to the selected topic.
Demonstrate professional responsibility and independent learning in communicating developments related to the selected topic.

courses.prerequisite_text: Senior level standing (completion of 90 credit hours)

SO1.statement: Ability to identify, formulate, and solve complex engineering problems by applying principles of engineering, science, and mathematics.
SO1.abet_illustration: Complex Engineering Problems – Complex engineering problems include one or more of the following characteristics: involving wide-ranging or conflicting technical issues; having no obvious solution; addressing problems not encompassed by current standards and codes; involving diverse groups of stakeholders; including many component parts or sub-problems; involving multiple disciplines; or having significant consequences in a range of contexts.

SO2.statement: An ability to apply engineering design to produce solutions that meet specified needs with consideration of public health, safety, and welfare, as well as global, cultural, social, environmental, and economic factors.
SO2.abet_illustration: Engineering design is a process of devising a system, component, or process to meet desired needs and specifications within constraints. It is an iterative, creative, decision-making process in which the basic sciences, mathematics, and engineering sciences are applied to convert resources into solutions. Engineering design involves identifying opportunities, developing requirements, performing analysis and synthesis, generating multiple solutions, evaluating solutions against requirements, considering risks, and making trade-offs, for the purpose of obtaining a high-quality solution under the given circumstances. Examples of possible constraints include aesthetics, codes, constructability, cost, ergonomics, extensibility, functionality, interoperability, legal considerations, maintainability, manufacturability, marketability, policy, regulations, schedule, standards, sustainability, or usability. This does not mean that each of these elements must have a significant effect on the design — it means the program must show that students consider these elements as they engage in design.

SO3.statement: An ability to communicate effectively with a range of audiences
SO3.abet_illustration: The “range of audiences” should include at least two distinct audiences relevant to the discipline or program’s mission. It is the program’s responsibility to determine the range of audiences (e.g., faculty, students, non-technical audiences, public sector, external clients, etc.).

SO4.statement: An ability to recognize ethical and professional responsibilities in engineering situations and make informed judgments, which must consider the impact of engineering solutions in global, economic, environmental, and societal contexts.
SO4.abet_illustration: Make informed judgments that consider the impact of engineering solutions in global, economic, environmental, and societal contexts. It is not necessary for every engineering situation to require that each context be a major consideration; consideration of impact as the judgment is made is key.

SO5.statement: An ability to function effectively on a team whose members together provide leadership, create a collaborative and inclusive environment, establish goals, plan tasks, and meet objectives.
SO5.abet_illustration: Student Outcome #5 requires students to function effectively on collaborative and inclusive teams and carry out project management tasks. Evidence may include instruments and artifacts such as Gantt charts, schedules, scrum, goal setting, decision matrices, and inclusiveness/collaboration measures.

SO6.statement: An ability to develop and conduct appropriate experimentation, analyze and interpret data, and use engineering judgment to draw conclusions.
SO6.abet_illustration: Student Outcome #6 requires the ability to develop and conduct appropriate experimentation, analyze and interpret data, and use engineering judgment to draw conclusions. There is no requirement that students be able to design an experiment. The components do not have to be addressed in series and may be satisfied in the context of more than one system.

SO7.statement: An ability to acquire and apply new knowledge as needed, using appropriate learning strategies.

PI11.statement: Identify the key requirements, interacting variables, and technical issues of a complex engineering problem.
PI11.course_level_guidance: For senior-level courses that include complex engineering problems.
PI11.abet_illustration:
Complex Engineering Problems – Complex engineering problems include one or more of the following characteristics: 
-involving wide-ranging or conflicting technical issues, 
-having no obvious solution, 
-addressing problems not encompassed by current standards and codes, 
-involving diverse groups of stakeholders, 
-including many component parts or sub-problems, 
-involving multiple disciplines, 
-or having significant consequences in a range of contexts.

PI12.statement: Formulate an engineering or mathematical model of a complex engineering problem using appropriate assumptions, parameters, and governing relationships.
PI12.course_level_guidance: For low-level courses such as circuits, electronics, signals, etc. Also for senior-level courses that include complex engineering problems (together with PI11).

PI13.statement: Solve the formulated complex engineering problem by applying appropriate principles of engineering, science, and mathematics using suitable analytical, computational, or experimental methods.

PI21.statement: Apply engineering design to produce a solution that meets specified needs
PI21.abet_illustration:
Engineering design is a process of devising a system, component, or process to meet desired needs and specifications within constraints. It is an iterative, creative, decision-making process in which the basic sciences, mathematics, and engineering sciences are applied to convert resources into solutions. Engineering design involves identifying opportunities, developing requirements, performing analysis and synthesis, generating multiple solutions, evaluating solutions against requirements, considering risks, and making trade-offs, for the purpose of obtaining a high-quality solution under the given circumstances. For illustrative purposes only, examples of possible constraints include aesthetics, codes, constructability, cost, ergonomics, extensibility, functionality, interoperability, legal considerations, maintainability, manufacturability, marketability, policy, regulations, schedule, standards, sustainability, or usability.

 This does not mean that each of these elements  (factors) must have a significant effect on the design — it just means that the program must show that students consider these elements as they engage in design.

PI22.statement: Design solutions that consider public health, safety, and welfare, as well as global, cultural, social, environmental, and economic factors.

PI23.statement: Identify and justify multiple realistic constraints relevant to the project design

PI24.statement: Identify and apply appropriate engineering standards and codes relevant to the project design.

PI31.statement: Communicate relevant, accurate, and sufficient engineering information.
PI31.abet_illustration:
-The guidance indicates that the “range of audiences” should include at least two distinct audiences (and they should be relevant to the discipline or program’s mission). 
-It is the program's responsibility to determine the range of audiences. For example, if a program stresses preparing students for graduate school, it might have students prepare a journal paper. There are many other possible audiences: faculty, students, non-technical, the public sector, etc. For example, students in biomedical engineering programs might communicate with doctors. In the major design experience, students might communicate with external clients. It is the program's responsibility to determine the most meaningful audiences for its students.

PI32.statement: Use appropriate communication methods and engineering representations to effectively convey information.

PI33.statement: Adapt communication to the knowledge and needs of different audiences.

PI41.statement: Recognize ethical and professional responsibilities in engineering situations
PI41.abet_illustration: make informed judgements that consider the impact of engineering solutions in global, economic, environmental, and societal contexts. It is not necessary for every engineering situation to require that each of these contexts be a major consideration. Consideration of the impact as the judgement is made is key.

PI42.statement: Make informed judgments considering the impact of engineering solutions in global, societal, economic, and environmental contexts

PI51.statement: Work effectively as a team member and contribute reliably to team tasks and objectives
PI51.abet_illustration: Student Outcome #5 requires that students be able to function effectively on collaborative and inclusive teams as well as carry out project management tasks. Programs have a variety of methods for demonstrating that students have these abilities. There are many texts on project management available for use. Gantt charts, schedules, scrum, goal setting, and decision matrices might be useful to demonstrate project management tasks. Inclusiveness and collaboration can be characterized using existing instruments in the literature.

PI52.statement: Provide leadership in planning and managing team work and support a collaborative, inclusive team environment
PI52.course_level_guidance: For senior-level courses that include a design project.

PI61.course_level_guidance: For senior-level courses that include experiment development.
PI61.abet_illustration:
Student Outcome #6 requires in part that students have the ability to develop and conduct appropriate experimentation, analyze and interpret data, and use engineering judgment to draw conclusions. There is no requirement that students be able to design an experiment. 

The components of Outcome 6 do not have to be addressed in series, and the outcome may be satisfied in the context of more than one system.

PI64.statement: Use engineering judgment to draw conclusions

PI71.statement: Acquire new knowledge using appropriate learning strategies

PI72.statement: Apply newly acquired knowledge to engineering tasks
